{
  "research_question": "How does mouse navigation performance vary across five different stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) when measured by Time-to-Target, Success rate, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "Sham stimulation produced the worst overall performance: lowest Success rate (0.273), highest Time-to-Target (4.68s), lowest Path Efficiency (0.308), lowest Average Speed (10.74), and lowest Angular Dispersion (0.236), suggesting minimal/no sensory feedback leads to slow, unsuccessful, and straighter but inefficient paths.",
    "Combined stimulation yielded the best or near-best performance on most metrics: high Success rate (0.780), fastest Time-to-Target (2.56s), high Path Efficiency (0.502), highest Average Speed (12.83), and highest Angular Dispersion (0.399), indicating multi-sensory integration supports optimal navigation.",
    "Bright Visual Only also performed well, with the highest Success rate (0.785) and relatively fast Time-to-Target (2.61s), comparable Path Efficiency (0.504) to Combined, and moderate Angular Dispersion (0.387), suggesting visual cues alone can nearly match multisensory performance.",
    "Dim Visual Only showed intermediate but notably poorer performance than Bright Visual: lower Success (0.673), slower Time-to-Target (3.14s), reduced Path Efficiency (0.434), slower speed (11.97), and lower Angular Dispersion (0.336), indicating visual stimulus intensity matters substantially.",
    "ICMS Only produced intermediate performance similar to Dim Visual Only: Success rate of 0.685, Time-to-Target of 3.05s, Path Efficiency of 0.432, Speed of 12.04, and Angular Dispersion of 0.354, suggesting intracortical microstimulation provides meaningful but suboptimal guidance compared to visual or combined modalities.",
    "Angular Dispersion tracked closely with overall performance quality: highest in successful/fast conditions (Combined, Bright Visual) and lowest in Sham, suggesting more angular exploration correlates with better target acquisition rather than inefficient meandering."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "Success rate: Sham (0.273) versus Combined (0.780) and Bright Visual Only (0.785) shows a 2.9-fold difference, the largest relative disparity across any metric.",
    "Time-to-Target: Sham (4.68s) was 1.8× slower than Combined (2.56s) and 1.5× slower than Bright Visual Only (2.61s), representing substantial behavioral slowing.",
    "Path Efficiency: Sham (0.308) versus Combined (0.502) and Bright Visual Only (0.504) shows a ~1.6× difference, indicating Sham produces notably more circuitous paths.",
    "Average Speed: Sham (10.74) versus Combined (12.83) represents a 19% reduction, smaller than other metrics but consistent with overall performance degradation.",
    "Angular Dispersion: Sham (0.236) versus Combined (0.399) shows a 1.7× difference, suggesting reduced active exploration or signal-driven path correction in the absence of stimulation."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "The data demonstrate clear sensory substitution and enhancement effects: any stimulation substantially outperforms Sham, with combined multimodal sensory feedback (visual + ICMS) generally producing optimal navigation. Bright visual cues alone nearly match combined performance, while dim visual or ICMS-only conditions produce intermediate but meaningful improvements over no stimulation. The 27% success rate in Sham versus 78% in Combined indicates sensory feedback is critical for this navigation task. Notably, higher angular dispersion correlates with better performance, suggesting that active, exploratory path correction—likely driven by received sensory feedback—facilitates target acquisition rather than indicating inefficient meandering.",
  "limitations": [
    "Sample sizes vary dramatically across paradigms (Combined n=48,846 vs. Sham n=3,505), which may affect estimate precision and comparability.",
    "No statistical testing (ANOVA, post-hoc comparisons, confidence intervals) has been performed; observed differences are descriptive only and significance is uncertain.",
    "Mouse-level clustering is evident (8 mice, n≈7,000–11,000 per mouse) but not accounted for; observations within mice are likely non-independent, potentially inflating apparent precision.",
    "Data are aggregated means without distributional information (variance, skew, outliers), possibly obscuring paradigm-dependent variability patterns.",
    "Temporal factors (learning, session order, fatigue) and potential interaction effects between stimulation parameters are not addressed in this summary.",
    "Angular dispersion interpretation as 'exploration' versus 'noise' is inferential without trajectory-level kinematic analysis."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Conduct mixed-effects models with random intercepts for Mouse to account for clustering, testing stimulation paradigm as a fixed effect on each performance variable; include post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey HSD) with multiplicity correction to identify which paradigm differences are statistically significant. Additionally, examine distributions and variance structures—particularly for Path Efficiency which shows extreme max values (29.8)—and consider modeling success as binary outcome using logistic regression. Finally, explore mouse-by-paradigm interaction effects to assess whether certain animals show idiosyncratic responses to specific stimulation types."
}
